Practical work No. 1

Familiarisation with portable dosimeters and training in their use

Purpose of work

To study the rules of work with dosimeters, their preparation for work and techniques of use.

Theory of work

Radioactivity is a phenomenon in which the nuclei of one chemical element spontaneously transform into nuclei of another element or isotopes of the same element. The process is accompanied by emission of particles and electromagnetic radiation.

Dosimetry is the determination of the dose of radioactive radiation absorbed by an object.

Radioactive radiation is not directly perceived by our senses. But it can be detected and measured indirectly.

Detection methods are based on the fact that radiation leaves a trace or is trapped in the matter through which it passes. The special detectors used today have different physical bases (gas, scintillation, semiconductor counters), but they use the same principle: they translate photons, electrons or alpha particles of radiation into an electrical signal to calculate the number of decays or in other words the number of becquerels.

Although 1 becquerel is an extremely small amount of radioactivity, the measuring instruments available to mankind are in most cases sensitive enough to detect radioactivity. Radioactivity can be measured either in the laboratory or with portable apparatus designed to record a specific type of radiation.

The three units of radioactivity are the becquerel, the gray and the sievert, in which radioactivity, its energy and exposure are measured, respectively (Table 43).

Table 43

Units of measurement of radioactivity

Measured value

Definition

Unit of measurement

Radioactivity

Number of decays per second

Becquerel (Bq)

Absorbed dose

Amount of energy received by matter from radiation

Grey (Gr).

Equivalent dose

Effects of radiation on the body

Sievert (Sv)

 

The activity in becquerels (Bq) is equal to the number of atoms decaying per second (1 Bq corresponds to the decay of one atom per second). Previously, the Curie unit was used to indicate the number of decays - corresponding to thirty-seven billion decays per second, named in honour of the discoverers of radium - Pierre and Marie Curie.

Gray (Gy) is a unit of measurement of the amount of energy released in a substance when exposed to radiation. 1 Gy corresponds to the fact that a substance has received one joule of energy per kilogramme of mass and determines the absorbed dose. Previously, the unit "rad" was used.

Sievert (Sv) is a unit of biological impact on the organism depending on the type of radiation. 1 sievert is the amount of energy absorbed by a kilogram of biological tissue, equal in effect to the absorbed dose of gamma radiation of 1 Gy. The equivalent dose, which characterises the biological effect of exposing an organism to ionising radiation, is measured in sieverts. Previously, the unit of Behr was used, which is 1 hundredth of a sievert. The annual average dose to the Earth's inhabitants from all sources is estimated at 2400 mR = 2.4 mSv.

Radiation monitoring is constantly carried out in Belarus. Information from the posts located throughout the country is updated once a day. At 12 of them, located near the Ignalina, Chernobyl, Rovno and Smolensk NPPs, measurements are taken every three hours. Data on the radiation background level in Belarus are also provided on the website of the Republican Hydrometeorological Centre

There are several types of dosimeters, some detect radiation in any objects, others detect a sudden change around and will tell you when this indicator will increase the norm, and there are those that quickly find radioactive objects at a great distance.

Household instruments usually have light and/or sound indication and a display for counting measurements. The size and design range from a wristband to a "pocket" version. Continuous operation time from a single battery is from a few hours to several months.

Gas-discharge indicators of ionising radiation based on the effect of avalanche breakdown of ionised space at field strength close to the critical field strength but not exceeding it are used as a radiation recording element in dosimeters. For this purpose, the field strength in the interelectrode space of the Geiger-Muller counter is maintained in the saturation state.

When ionising radiation enters the sensor space, forced ionisation (appearance of free charge carriers) occurs under its influence and avalanche breakdown occurs in the charged electric field along the track. Let us consider the main types of dosimeters.

Dosimeter alarm. It is a device that will immediately notice fluctuations of radiation around you and, if they increase and exceed the norm, will inform you about it with an alarm.

An indicator and a meter are roughly similar. Both types can tell you if there is radioactivity in a thing. But meters are very accurate and can even detect radiation in the soil, whether it is there or not.

Finder. The device does not report changes in radioactive indicators around, but can find any anomaly, ore and other things. More useful for serious research and experiments.

Practical work №3

Relative humidity measurement

Objective: to master the methods of determining the relative humidity of air, based on the use of different designs of hygrometers and psychrometers.

Air humidity is measured using hygrometers (Greek: ὑ γρός - wet) and psychrometers (υστρός-cold).

Theory of work. Knowing only the absolute humidity, you can not tell whether the air is dry or wet, how close it is to the state of saturation. Most often, the water vapor contained in the air is unsaturated. If water vapor in the air was always saturated, then everything on the earth's surface would never dry up.

Air humidity has two quantitative characteristics: absolute and relative humidity.

Relative humidity describes the moisture content compared to the maximum amount of moisture that can be contained in a given substance in a state of thermodynamic equilibrium. Such a macroscopic system can be a single body (for example, a gas, a liquid, and a vapor in equilibrium with it). Thus, relative humidity is the ratio of the amount of water vapor actually present in the air to the maximum possible amount at a given temperature (Table 47).

Relative humidity is measured as a percentage and the symbol φ is used to indicate it.

The vital activity of animals and plant organisms is possible only in certain ranges of temperature and humidity. Humidity can make a significant error in the weight of the object. A kilogram of sugar or grain with a moisture content of 5% and 10% will contain different amounts of dry sugar or grain.

The relative humidity of the air in the service area and the residential area of public buildings, at workplaces in premises, at consumer service enterprises, in locomotive cabins, etc., etc. is regulated by Sanitary rules and regulations. Permissible values of relative humidity in the workplace in the premises are 15-75%, in residential areas and the serviced area of public buildings 30-60%.

Most people feel most comfortable at temperatures between + 20 and +22 °C and relative humidity between 40 and 60 %. If the relative humidity value falls below 30 %, as it happens during the heating season, problems begin: dry air tends to absorb as much moisture as possible, which it takes away from the environment, including people in it.

As a result, skin itching, burning in the eyes, headache and general fatigue may appear – this is how dehydration manifests itself.

You can change the humidity of the indoor air. Humidifiers are used to increase humidity. Functions of dehumidification (lowering humidity) of air are implemented in most air conditioners and in the form of separate devices-осушителей dehumidifiers.

The principle of operation of the August psychrometer is described in Figure145.

The August psychrometer consists of two thermometers: dry and wet. A wet thermometer shows a lower temperature than a dry one, since its tank is wrapped in a cloth soaked in water, which cools it down by evaporating. The evaporation rate depends on the relative humidity of the air.

Water from the fabric evaporates, which causes the thermometer to cool down. The process continues until the steam near the wet cloth reaches saturation and the thermometer shows the dew point temperature. A wet thermometer shows a temperature less than or equal to the actual ambient temperature. The second thermometer remains dry and shows the actual temperature

The variety of hygrometer models is constantly expanding. The operation of hygrometers is based on variations in the physical parameters of different materials. When the amount of vapor in the air changes, the properties change: density, weight, length, and other operating parameters of substances. By recording changes in the physical characteristics of materials, we can draw conclusions about the amount of vapor in the air.

Piezoelectric hygrometers, which record changes in the frequency of mechanical vibrations of a piezoelectric plate (quartz crystal) with a film of a reversibly absorbing substance applied to it, have become widespread. When moisture is absorbed, the mass of the film increases, and the frequency of vibrations of the electromechanical system decreases.

Recently, integrated humidity sensors (usually with voltage output) have become widely used, based on the property of some polymers to change their electrical characteristics (such as the permittivity of the medium) under the influence of water vapor contained in the air.

Digital moisture meters work with microchips, so calculations are made within a few seconds, and the output data has a minimum error. When determining air humidity with this type of device, the ambient temperature must be taken into account. The smallest deviations from stationary conditions affect the final indicators, so before direct measurement, street doors must be closed for 15 minutes.

PRACTICAL WORK №5

Protozoa personal respiratory protection equipment

Purpose of the work

Mastering the techniques of using the simplest personal respiratory protection equipment.

Brief theoretical information

In an emergency situation, there may be a situation where it is necessary to protect the respiratory organs from harmful impurities, but industrial-made personal respiratory protection equipment will not be at hand. Therefore, each person should be able to make the simplest means of protection: cotton-gauze bandages or anti-dust fabric masks. They reliably protect the respiratory organs (as well as the skin of the face and eyes) from radioactive dust and harmful aerosols. However, they do not protect against many toxic substances.

In the civil defense system for the adult population, in addition to gas masks, anti–dust fabric masks PTM-1 and cotton-gauze bandages made by the population can also be widely used to protect the respiratory system from the ingress of radioactive dust and bacterial agents–.

In addition to activated carbon, fibrous materials (Petryanov fabric, PVC perchloride, etc.) are used to purify the air from harmful aerosol impurities. These materials are most commonly used in respirators and filter protective clothing.

The anti-dust fabric mask (Figure 151) consists of a housing 1 and a mount 3. In the body of the mask, viewing holes are made, where 2 glasses (plexiglass, celluloid plates) are inserted. The body of the mask is made of 4-5 layers of fabric: the outer layer is made of loose fabric (calico, cotton cloth or other fabrics; the inner layers (2-3) are made of denser fabrics (flannel, baize, cloth, cotton or woolen fabric with fleece). The layer adjacent to the face can be made of satin, calico. Fixing the mask is made from a single layer of any fabric, but best of all from lining or linen. The tight fit of the mask to the face eliminates the penetration of contaminated air under it, and this is ensured by a rubber band 4 threaded into the upper seam, and ties 6 sewn to the lower seam of the attachment, as well as a transverse elastic band 5 attached to the upper corners of the mask body.

Fig. 151. Anti-dust fabric mask

To avoid infection with a dangerous virus with all its complications, you need to protect yourself in any possible way. A cotton-gauze bandage is an elementary means of protecting the respiratory system. If you do not have gauze at hand, you can also make a bandage from a bandage.

A cotton gauze bandage is the simplest and most affordable means of protecting the respiratory tract from various bacteria and infections. It is also necessary when someone in the family is already ill, and you do not want the rest of the family to get infected.

Making the simplest cotton-gauze mask

https://youtu.be/MKlFbCmMntk://youtu.be/MKlFbCmMntk Video 45 sec

In order for a gauze product to serve as a prevention of viral diseases, you need to know how to properly put it on and wear it. When used correctly, this affordable product can reliably protect against germs.

Personal respiratory protection equipment must cover not only the nose, but also the mouth. Tie it tightly, but not too tightly, so that there is no discomfort. You need to wear a mask when you go to the store or transport. If you are at work or other public places, the bandage is changed every 2 hours, otherwise the bacteria that we want to protect ourselves from will accumulate on it. If you are at home or on the street during the epidemic, the bandage can be changed every 3-4–hours.

Task 1

Application of an anti-dust fabric mask

The mask (see Figure 151) is put on as follows: remove the headdress, transfer the cross elastic band and the mask mount to the outer side of it, take both hands by the lower edge of the mount so that the thumbs are facing out, tightly apply the lower part of the mask body to the chin, remove the mount behind the head and press the mask tightly with the palms face. Then tie the ends of the occipital ties and pull a transverse elastic band over the head. The viewing holes of the mask should be placed strictly against the eyes. After that, put on a headdress.

Task 2

Methods of making cotton-gauze bandages.

At your discretion, use one of the suggested methods to make a bandage (from gauze or bandages).

Option 1. The bandage is made from a piece of gauze measuring 100 x 50 cm (Figure152). In the middle, put an even layer of cotton wool measuring 20 x 20 cm, 1–2cm thick. On both sides, the gauze is bent along the entire length, superimposing on cotton wool. The remaining ends of the gauze are cut into 30-35–cm on each side for tying. End sheathing is allowed.

Figure152. Technology of manufacturing a cotton-gauze dressing (option 1)

Option 2. You will need: 2 bandages 14 cm wide and 7 m long; package of hygienic medical cotton wool (100 grams). Put cotton wool measuring 14 x 14 cm on the edge of a 60 cm long bandage, tuck it in the bandage 3 times. The second bandage should be cut lengthwise into two parts. Each half is twisted for ties, they are threaded at the top and bottom, bandages are sewn. The output is 12-14–dressings.

Option 3. Take two long strips of 70-90–cm bandage and roll them up 3 times. Sew them along the entire length. You can make it by hand or stitch it on a typewriter. Take 4 identical pieces of gauze 17x17cm. Place a cotton square between the 2 layers and cover with the remaining 2 layers of gauze. Sew a basting seam around the edges. Tuck the edges inwards by 1 cm and gently stitch. On the finished mask, sew long ties along the length, so that one is on top, the other on the bottom. They must be the same length.

Practical work №6

Cleaning of gases from dust and smoke during fuel combustion

Purpose of the work

Consider methods for protecting the air pool from the effects of harmful substances generated during fuel combustion.

Theory of operation

To protect the air pool from exposure to harmful substances generated during fuel combustion, the following measures are applied:

  • greening of technological processes;
  • cleaning of gas emissions released into the atmosphere.

Greening of technological processes involves the creation of closed technological cycles, waste-free and low-waste technologies that exclude harmful pollutants from entering the atmosphere, replacing local boiler plants with centralized heat, preliminary purification of fuel and raw materials from harmful impurities, replacing coal and fuel oil with natural gas, etc. Partial recirculation, i.e. the reuse of waste gases with subsequent purification, is becoming increasingly common.

Various methods of cleaning waste gases from dust, ash, soot and toxic gas and vapor impurities (NO, NO2, SO2, SO3, etc) are widely used at enterprises.

Consider the principle of operation of some devices for cleaning exhaust gases. The design of these devices depends on the degree of dust in the air, the size of solid particles and the required level of cleaning.

Dry dust collectors (cyclones, precipitation chambers, filters, etc.) are designed for rough mechanical cleaning of emissions from coarse and heavy dust. The principle of operation is the settling of particles under the action of centrifugal forces and gravity. The dust and gas stream is introduced into the cyclone through the branch pipe 2 (Figure 153, a). Then it performs a rotational-translational movement along the body. Dust particles are thrown against the walls 1of the cyclone housing 1 and then fall down into the dust collector (hopper 4), from where they are periodically removed. The purified gas 3is released into the atmosphere through the central branch pipe 3. To increase the efficiency of work, group (battery) cyclones are used. The appearance of the cyclone is shown in Fig. 153, b.

The simplicity of the design, as well as environmental friendliness, contribute to the spread of devices in industries in various fields. Dry mechanical dust collectors are necessary for processing air masses in production facilities. In the course of working processes, a huge amount of dust and impurities consisting of microscopic particles are produced. Their total mass can be measured in tens of kilograms per day

a)

b)

Fig. 153. Diagram of the cyclone device (a); its appearance (b).

" Wet " dust collectors (scrubbers) require water supply and work on the principle of deposition of dust particles on the surface of droplets under the action of inertia and Brownian motion. Scrubbers provide 99 % cleaning of particles larger than 2 microns and, like all dust collectors of this type, are indispensable for cleaning dust from explosive and hot gases. "Wet" dust collectors allow not only to purify gases, but also to cool them and, if necessary, to dispose of their heat. Such dust collectors are relatively inexpensive.

Fig. 154. Venturi scrubber (operating principle)

Venturi scrubbers (Figure 154) –are high (up to 30 m) towers in which dusty gas is introduced tangentially to the tower wall. Their effect is based on the Venturi effect, which is a drop in pressure when a liquid or gas stream flows through a narrowed part of the pipe. This effect is named after the Italian physicist Giovanni Venturi. Sprayed liquid or foam is fed into the raw gas stream through the nozzles. The purified gas is removed from the top of the unit, and water with trapped dust is collected at the bottom of the scrubber.

Passing through the narrow section of the Venturi pipe, the flow enters the wide part of the scrubber. As the pipe cross-section increases, the gas velocity decreases and a large number of microscopic liquid droplets adhere to solid dirt, increasing their volume and weight.

Such gas purifiers are widely used in the metallurgical, chemical, and energy industries, as well as in the production of bulk building materials and fertilizers.

Electrofilters are the most advanced method for cleaning gases from suspended dust particles up to 0.01 microns in size, with a high efficiency of gas purification (99.0-99.5 %). The principle of operation of all types of electrostatic precipitators is based on the ionization of the dust and gas flow at the surface of the corona electrodes. Acquiring a negative charge, dust motes move to the precipitation electrode, which has a sign opposite to the charge of the corona electrode. When the electrodes are shaken, the deposited dust particles fall down into the dust collector due to gravity. Electrodes require a large amount of electricity consumption – this is their main drawback.

Electric filters have a high throughput capacity (unlike other dust collectors, they have no hydraulic resistance).

Methods for cleaning emissions from toxic gas and vapor impurities (NO, NO2, SO2, etc.) are divided into groups:

  • absorption of impurities by applying catalytic conversion;
  • washing of emissions with impurity solvents (absorption method);
  • absorption of gaseous impurities by solids with an ultramicroporous structure (adsorption method).

Using the catalytic method, toxic components of industrial emissions are converted into substances that are harmless or less harmful to the environment by introducing additional substances called catalysts into the system. Palladium-containing and vanadium catalysts are widely used. With their help, carbon monoxide is catalytically burned to dioxide and sulfur dioxide to oxide.

The absorption method is based on the absorption of harmful gaseous impurities by a liquid absorber (absorbent). As an absorbent, water, solutions of alkalis, ammonia and others are used in devices where the absorption process is carried out, called an absorber.

The adsorption method allows the extraction of harmful components using adsorbents – solids with an ultra-microporous structure (activated carbon and alumina, silica gel). For example, at nuclear power plants (NPPs), the method of purification of process gases by sorption of radioactive products on coal filters – adsorbents is widely used, which can reliably prevent atmospheric pollution in all operating modes of nuclear power plants.

Task 1

Demonstration of the action of the beekeeper's smoker.

For subsequent experiments, smoke production is required. The principle of the simplest modern design is a metal base with a spout. Fuel material is placed inside. Through the flask, air is supplied by a fan, so that smoke comes out of the spout.

Bee smoke sprayer can be filled with absolutely any raw material – paper, dry grass, hay, straw, pine branches and cones. The procedure for lighting the smoker;

  • Start a fire in the combustion cup by placing a small amount of organic fuel (paper) inside.
  • Turn on the device.
  • When the smoke starts coming in, close the lid.
  • Connect the fan.

Figure 155-An electrified beekeeper's smoker for conducting experiments.

Note. In order not to use smoke from cigarettes or their electronic analogues, it is suggested to use an ecological beekeeper's smoker. Passive cigarette smoke enters the body in three ways: by ingestion, inhalation, and absorption. You can swallow nicotine and other chemicals from cigarette smoke if you touch a surface contaminated with cigarette smoke and put your hand to your mouth.

Task 2

Demonstration of the operation of a chimney.

Simple equipment is required to demonstrate the formation of draft in the chimney: 1) a glass tube with a length of 30-40–cm and a diameter of about 6 cm; 2) a spirit lamp; 3) a smoker; 4) a turntable on a wire holder; 5) a universal tripod.

Collects a model of a chimney installation (Figure 156). The spirit lamp is placed at such a height that its flame does not enter the pipe.

First, take the spirit lamp aside and light it. You should pay attention to the size of the flame – it should be quite wide and low. After that, put a spirit lamp under the pipe, as shown in the figure, and observe that the flame is noticeably stretched up. Adjust the position of the pipe (or alcohol lamp) so that the alcohol lamp burns evenly and calmly.

Then, from the smoker located on the side of the installation, a uniform stream of smoke is released from below. They observe how the smoke is quickly drawn together with the cold air into the pipe and rushes up it, carried away by the heated air.

Figure 156. Model of the chimney.

Figure 157. Patterns for making turntables (a) and snakes (b).

In this experiment, it is convenient to use a turntable or a snake attached to the tip of a wire holder to detect traction. Placed above the pipe is shown in Figure 156 as a dotted line, the pinwheel comes into rotation. If you move the pipe away from the spirit lamp, then the turntable will not rotate at the same height (but without the pipe). Pinwheel and snake patterns are shown in Figure 157.

The turntable can be made from thick paper or aluminum foil. You need to cut out a circle with a diameter of 80-100 mm and enter a circle with a radius of 15-20–mm. Then divide the circle into 10-12 parts and cut it along the radial lines to a small circle. The resulting petals are slightly bent relative to their longitudinal axis. In the center of the disk, make a small recess for support. Instead of a turntable, you can make a simple light snake.

Task 3

Demonstration of the attraction of gases by an electrified body.

The experience will require equipment: 1) a stick for electrification; 2)a device for obtaining nitrogen dioxide; 3) a universal tripod; 4) nitric acid; 5) copper sawdust.

A distinctive feature by which one can judge the electrification of a particular body is the attraction of other bodies by the latter. An electrified body attracts both light and heavy bodies, liquid and gaseous bodies.

158. Attraction of gases by an electrified body:

a is the first stage of experience;

b is the second stage of experience.

To demonstrate the attraction of gases in a special vessel (figure 6) pour copper sawdust and fill it with nitric acid. As a result of the reaction between copper and acid, nitrogen dioxide NO2 is released, which has a bright brown color that is clearly visible on a white background. Opening the tap, observe the flow of nitrogen dioxide from the vessel (see Figure 158, a). Having brought an electrified stick to the gas jet, they notice the attraction of gas to it (see Figure 158, b).

When setting up this experiment, it should be borne in mind that inhaling significant amounts of nitrogen dioxide is harmful, so the devices should be installed in a fume hood. Alternatively, the experiment can be conducted directly with the smoker.

Task 4

Demonstration of the principle of operation of the electrostatic precipitator.

For experiments, you will need: 1) a wide-necked jar with a stopper; 2) a glass tube with a length of 30-40–cm and a diameter of about 6 cm; 3) a smoker; 4) universal laboratory rectifier or electrophoretic machine; 5) connecting wires and copper wire; 6) universal tripod.

The principle of operation of the electrostatic precipitator can be demonstrated using the installation shown in Figure 159. In the cork of a glass jar, two holes are made at the greatest possible distance from each other and electrodes (copper wire) are passed through them. The jar is filled with smoke and closed with a cork so that the ends of the wires do not close together. The electrodes are connected by wires to a high-voltage rectifier or conductors of an electrophoretic machine. After applying a high voltage to the electrodes, the smoke disappears.

Fig. 159. Demonstration of smoke cleaning with an electric filter.

Fig. 160. Demonstration of the device and operation of the electrostatic precipitator.

To be convincing, the experiment can be conducted twice. This phenomenon is explained by the appearance of a corona discharge in the conductors. In the electric field, gas ions move between the wire electrodes, but they collide with the smoke-forming particles and charge them. Charged smoke particles under the action of an electric field move to the electrodes and settle on them.

Using the equipment used to demonstrate the operation of the chimney, you can make a model of an industrial electrostatic precipitator and show its operation (Figure-160).

Inside the glass tube, a long narrow salt ribbon is stretched along its wall. On an insulated rod located above the tube, a thin wire is suspended with a ball or a suitable weight at the end. The wire should be located along the axis of the tube and not touch its walls (especially for the staniol tape). The ends of the wire and staniol tape are connected by conductors to a high-voltage rectifier.

We observe that when the rectifier is connected, the gas in the tube is cleared of smoke particles supplied from below from the smoker.

Practical lesson №7

The topic is " Determination of the natural light coefficient (KEO)"

Purpose of the work. 1) Learn how to work with a lux meter. 2) Determination of KEO using instruments. 3) Assessment of indoor lighting by comparing the actual KEO values with the normalized ones.

Theoretical background of the work. In accordance with the determination of the natural illumination coefficient (KEO) by the formula KEO = to obtain its values in full-scale conditions, natural illumination measurements are made indoors and on a horizontal open area under the natural sky. When processing measurements using this formula, it is necessary to measure the value of outdoor illumination and indoor lighting simultaneously. This synchronization is necessary because the outdoor illumination may change over a short period of time (for example, an increase in cloud cover).

In accordance with the requirement of natural lighting standards for buildings, KEO are determined at at least five points in the characteristic section of the room. As a rule, such a section should run in a straight line perpendicular to the plane of the window through its center. The two extreme points are located at a distance of 1 m from the outer and opposite inner walls, respectively. In the interval between them, there are at least three points at equal distances from each other. The height of the points above the floor level of the room should be 0.8 m. At this height there is a so-called conditional working surface. Points are numbered starting from the window.

It is not recommended to take measurements when the sky is clear, when the sun is in the part of the sky where the window opening is oriented.

Appliances and accessories: 1) luxmeters – 2 pcs.; 2) screen for the outdoor photocell of the luxmeter; 3) tripod fixing the horizontal position of the photocell of the luxmeter; 4) tape measure; 5) clock-2 pcs.

When carrying out work, you should use luxmeters of the type U-16 or U–116. These devices are portable and are designed to measure the illumination created by incandescent, fluorescent and natural daylight lamps.in a large range.

U–17 type luxmeters are designed to measure the illumination of streets, territories of factories and construction sites, railway stations, etc. under night lighting, that is, low illumination (the upper limit is 100 lux). Since this device is designed to work at low light levels, its use in this practical work is not allowed.

The U–116 device (Figure – 161) is equipped with an iron-selenium photocell, to which a sensitive galvanometer is connected using a flexible conductor.

Fig. 161– U-116 Luxmeter

The device has switches and scales corresponding to the measurement ranges, graded in lux by a standard source with a radiation spectrum approaching that of medium-power incandescent lamps. The photocell of the lux meter does not have a light filter, so when measuring illumination from sources that significantly differ in spectral composition from incandescent lamps, correction factors should be entered. For example, with fluorescent lamps LD – 0,9, with LB-1,1.

162. Luxmeter assembled from demonstration physical devices.

To increase the accuracy of measurements and avoid introducing correction factors, more accurate luxmeters have yellow-green filters that have reduced transmission in the violet and red parts of the spectrum.

When performing work, instead of special luxmeters, you can use an installation assembled from a demonstration photocell and a galvanometer (included in the set of devices of the physical office). If the scale of the galvanometer is pre-graded in terms of illumination units using a reference device, you will get a measuring device – a luxmeter (Figure 162). In the absence of a reference device, the work is carried out efficiently (without specific numerical values of illumination).

Task 1.

Performing illumination measurements.

Illumination on an outdoor open horizontal platform and at points in the room is measured simultaneously. Simultaneous measurements can be carried out in time (using a clock), visually (by sending signals through a window in line of sight), or by mobile phone. The measurement results are recorded in a pre-prepared table. When processing measurement results using the formula, simultaneous values of external and internal illumination are used.

Fig. 163. Shading of a photocell when measuring ambient ambient light.

When measuring outdoor illumination, it is necessary to make sure that direct sunlight does not fall on the photocell. If outdoor illumination is measured on an open horizontal platform in clear weather, then direct sunlight should be cut off by a special shading screen (Figure 163), the diameter of which should be equal to two diameters of the photocell. The distance from the screen to the photocell is kept constant by means of a thin rod on a hinged support, the length of which for the photocell of the U–116 luxmeter is 135 cm.

The results of measurements in this paper should be summarized in the form of two graphs of light distribution dependencies in the room: E = f(l) and KEO =f(l), where E is the illumination (lux) at different points of the room, starting from the window; l is the distance (m) from the window; KEO is the coefficient of natural illumination (%).

Based on the results of the study, we can draw a conclusion about the dependence of the illumination E and the natural illumination coefficient

KEO on the distance l to the light source (window).

Task 2

Comparison of the efficiency of incandescent and fluorescent lamps.

Completing task 2 clearly shows the advantage of fluorescent lamps over incandescent lamps. It is necessary to measure and compare the illumination from two lamps of different types, but the same power.

Task 3

Investigation of the light flux distribution around an electric lamp.

Task 3 requires additional instrumentation. Figure 164 shows an installation consisting of an autotransformer for adjusting the brightness of the incandescent lamp, an optical disk with a photocell, and a demonstration galvanometer connected to the photocell.

Fig. 164. Installation for demonstrating the distribution of the light flux around an electric lamp.

The initial brightness of the lamp is selected using an autotransformer so that the galvanometer needle does not deviate beyond the scale. Then the holder with the photocell is slowly rotated around the burning lamp and the° galvanometer readings are recorded every 20°. According to the obtained data, the light flux distribution curve in polar coordinates is drawn in the notebook (Figure-165). On the coordinate grid, the readings of the galvanometer at different positions of the photocell for a full revolution are postponed along the radii. In the above graphs, the light flux distribution diagram for lamps with frosted glass is shown by line b, the second diagram (line a) is drawn for a lamp with ordinary transparent glass.

Figure 165. Diagrams of the light flux distribution of electric lamps.

From the conducted studies, when comparing diagrams, it follows that lamps made of frosted or milky glass have a more uniform distribution of the light flux (and do not affect vision so much).
